# Research

I work on mathematical modeling, uncertainty quantification, optimization, and statistical methodology. My research combines mechanistic models with computational analysis to understand biological systems and support decisions when data are limited and parameters are uncertain.

- [Triple-negative breast cancer](#tnbc)

<a id="tnbc"></a>

## Triple-negative breast cancer

Which interactions in the tumor microenvironment most strongly impact tumor size? In this collaborative project, we developed an ordinary differential equation model of five cell populations and their interactions: tumor cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts, M2 macrophages, cytotoxic T lymphocytes, and regulatory T cells.

We used global sensitivity analysis to identify influential model parameters. The model provides a framework for generating therapeutic hypotheses and investigating combinations of treatment targets.

<a id="melanoma"></a>

## Rare melanomas

This work uses canine melanoma as a comparative oncology model, combining RNA-sequencing data and biological literature to build a mechanistic model of melanoma–immune interactions.

<a id="liver"></a>

## Liver transplantation

Transplant immunology · Dynamical systems · Sensitivity analysis

While short term outcoms for liver-transplant patients have improved, long-term outcomes have not. There is a delicate balance of adequate levels of immune suppression to prevent rejection, and avoiding weakening the immune system too much. Our goal in this work was to identify key pathways in long-term liver transplant immune dynamics. 

Sensitivity analysis identified dynamics associated with cytotoxic T cells, IL-2, and the liver itself as important determinants of graft injury. This work lays a foundation for future model calibration and studies of immunosuppression, with the longer-term goal of balancing rejection risk against treatment toxicity.

<a id="dyadic-cart"></a>

## Statistical methodology: Dyadic CART

Blackwell Summer Scholars, UIUC · Summer 2021<br>With Sophia Sohail; mentored by Dr. Sabyasachi Chatterjee

During the Blackwell Summer Scholars program at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, I worked on nonparametric distributional regression using Dyadic CART. The goal was to estimate conditional cumulative distribution functions, capturing information about a response beyond its conditional mean.

My work included implementing two-fold cross-validation and distributional regression procedures in R. We evaluated the method using simulated data and a height–weight dataset, and used estimated conditional distributions to construct prediction intervals.
